# 17. Community and business

Roguelikes are mostly played alone, but they are understood together. A run becomes a story when someone else hears it; a strange death becomes knowledge when someone else learns from it; a balance change becomes an argument. This chapter covers everything that happens around the game rather than inside it: the tools that let players share runs, play online, mod and follow development, the work of reading feedback and tending a community, and the business questions of who the game is for, how it gets found, how it pays and who owns what a community builds.

It matters to someone making a roguelike because the talks treat these as design decisions, not afterthoughts. Whether your game writes a log, accepts a seed or keeps its content in data files decides what your community can do with it, and the same community that retells runs is also the one that streams, crowdfunds, buys and argues about the game. The first half of the chapter is about building and keeping that community; the second half is about the business that rests on it. Much of the material comes from people who ran servers, wikis, Discords and campaigns, so it is unusually concrete, and where it rests on a single case the text says so.

## In brief

- Procedural variety earns its keep when players can compare, retell and argue about their runs, so the community is part of the design, not an audience for it ([Tariq et al. 2016, 2:03](https://youtu.be/SDojcmObQzw?t=123); [Ivy Melinda 2020, 7:55](https://youtu.be/db6S2lgTWmI?t=475); [Joel Clark 2020, 17:55](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=1075); [Julian Day 2020, 13:21](https://youtu.be/aBbaUSWFQPM?t=801); [Various 2018, 15:46](https://youtu.be/60MTG-__dt4?t=946)).
- Build the means of sharing into the game from the start: logs and scrollback that are easy to read and pass on, seeds, morgue files and safe public data, inspected at the cropped scale players actually share ([Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi 2021, 15:40](https://youtu.be/WeRCGy3-uPY?t=940); [Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi 2021, 7:40](https://youtu.be/WeRCGy3-uPY?t=460); [Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi 2021, 21:26](https://youtu.be/WeRCGy3-uPY?t=1286); [Alan Malloy 2017, 9:35](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=575); [Mike Cook 2026, 22:02](https://youtu.be/nOGNdrjm8ek?t=1322)).
- Putting a single-player roguelike online need not change its rules, yet spectating, shared servers and scoreboards bring reach, data and social space and can cut the learning curve from years to weeks ([Alan Malloy 2017, 0:30](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=30); [Drew Streib 2016, 11:44](https://youtu.be/J4RK-3zW8vY?t=704)).
- Keeping content in data files, ideally alongside scripting, lets players mod the game, makes mods more robust to updates, and helps the community build itself ([Ray 2023, 7:58](https://youtu.be/n6mKigS_71Y?t=478); [George Moromisato 2022, 18:31](https://youtu.be/mES03vaZo3U?t=1111); [Josh Ge 2016, 6:48](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=408); [Dylan Gedig 2022, 13:14](https://youtu.be/ke0cLTVg2_M?t=794)).
- Roguelikes suit open development because the same players replay every change, so release early and often, put feedback one click away and visibly credit what you act on ([Chris King 2022, 1:00](https://youtu.be/1Np1DSdpoR0?t=60); [Josh Ge 2018, 25:15](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=1515); [Chris King 2022, 4:35](https://youtu.be/1Np1DSdpoR0?t=275); [Chris King 2022, 6:22](https://youtu.be/1Np1DSdpoR0?t=382); [Brian Cronin 2025, 26:33](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=1593)).
- Treat every complaint as valid information about a player's experience but not as an instruction: find the desire behind it, diagnose it, and weigh the quiet players who are not complaining before you change course ([Evan Debenham 2021, 11:42](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=702); [Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 9:37](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=577); [Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 19:48](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=1188); [Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 25:51](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=1551); [Dan DiIorio 2025, 3:10](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=190)).
- A community left to form by itself ends up run by its loudest, meanest voices, so cultivate it deliberately and budget the time it costs ([Caelyn Sandel 2020, 22:15](https://youtu.be/NANqgqeqh2k?t=1335); [Ivy Melinda 2020, 0:54](https://youtu.be/db6S2lgTWmI?t=54); [Chris King 2022, 13:42](https://youtu.be/1Np1DSdpoR0?t=822)).
- In the cases the talks describe, streamers, festivals and an existing community sold the games far more than social media did, so plan updates and demos around the creators who will show them ([Dylan Gedig 2022, 3:36](https://youtu.be/ke0cLTVg2_M?t=216); [Dylan Gedig 2022, 9:05](https://youtu.be/ke0cLTVg2_M?t=545); [Philomena Schwab 2024, 8:50](https://youtu.be/MTam5RT8Kn0?t=530); [Dylan Gedig 2022, 20:49](https://youtu.be/ke0cLTVg2_M?t=1249); [Evan Debenham 2021, 4:21](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=261)).
- Keep monetisation away from the challenge and expect to earn the right to charge, since ads intrude and pay-for-advantage cheapens a hard game ([Evan Debenham 2021, 19:48](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=1188); [Evan Debenham 2021, 23:08](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=1388); [Philomena Schwab 2024, 10:58](https://youtu.be/MTam5RT8Kn0?t=658)).
- Crowdfunding cannot build a community, only draw on one, and in ADOM's campaign the developer's own outreach, not the platform, was the biggest source of donations ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 12:44](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=764); [Thomas Biskup 2017, 5:27](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=327)).

## Why a single-player genre lives in its community

Most roguelikes are played by one person at a keyboard, yet the talks keep returning to the claim that the meaning of a run is made afterwards, among other people. This section sets out why that matters for design.

### Procedural variety needs someone to compare it with

Several speakers, working on very different games, reach the same conclusion: procedural generation earns its keep when players can compare what happened to them. Tariq, the developer of Catacomb Kids, reasoned from a thought experiment about removing procedural variation from life itself: different choices only matter if you can talk to someone else about how yours went, so procedural generation without a community to discuss the differences loses much of its point ([Tariq et al. 2016, 2:03](https://youtu.be/SDojcmObQzw?t=123)). Ivy Melinda, community manager of Caves of Qud, describes the same mechanism from the other side. Because systems, procgen and emergent narrative give every player a different take on the story, the places where interpretations do not overlap are the most fertile ground for fan art, mods and fiction, and those works feed back into the game in what Melinda calls a social ecology ([Ivy Melinda 2020, 7:55](https://youtu.be/db6S2lgTWmI?t=475)). Joel Clark makes the strongest version of the claim for Blaseball, a game of forces deliberately out of the players' control: alone it would be insufferable, together players wade through it and work things out faster ([Joel Clark 2020, 17:55](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=1075)).

> I think the number one path through chaos is community. — [Joel Clark 2020, 17:55](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=1075)

The common thread is that randomness produces differences, and differences only become interesting once someone else can see them. A run that nobody else hears about is a private event; a run compared, argued over and retold becomes part of a shared body of knowledge.

### Mythmaking is the genre's culture

Julian Day argues that mythmaking is central to roguelikes, and that it happens less in the games than in the community, which retells the stories of memorable characters and deaths on forums, Twitter and, earlier, newsgroups. Day's example is Dwarf Fortress succession games, where one save file was passed between players and the resulting tales became shared experience for participants and readers alike ([Julian Day 2020, 13:21](https://youtu.be/aBbaUSWFQPM?t=801)). Kawa makes the same point about death specifically: Yet Another Silly Death posts, looted screenshots and Boatmurdered are what players do when they are not playing, and Kawa calls storytelling the third function of a morgue file (the text record a game writes when a character dies), something games should actively support ([Various 2018, 15:46](https://youtu.be/60MTG-__dt4?t=946)). The storytelling extends into fiction: Kyla read a 2015 NetHack fan story written as the Oracle's diary, built from the game's fortune-cookie rumours and its dungeon inhabitants, in which the Oracle's statues are smashed by an adventurer and she responds by ordering statue traps ([Thomas Robertson et al. 2017, 10:18](https://youtu.be/H6fPIhLoA1Y?t=618)).

The designer's side of this is a kind of letting go. Dan DiIorio observes that players of Luck be a Landlord do not feel it is a game made by its developer but one they played; once released, their experiences belong to them, especially in a roguelike with endless possibilities, and DiIorio has had to accept that others will build on what has been let go ([Dan DiIorio 2025, 17:45](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=1065)).

### Communities that generate play and give people something

Some communities go further and produce the play itself. Stella Mazeika notes that every randomizer (a tool that reshuffles a classic game's items or layout into a new run) has grown a community that organises races, teaches newcomers, hosts events and gets races into larger events; for Mazeika, the lesson is that software is made out of people and inclusive communities around it are essential ([Stella Mazeika 2019, 13:29](https://youtu.be/C7laugXEc9s?t=809)). Nat Alison offers a human alternative to procgen altogether. The hand-crafted variant sudoku community grew rapidly from 2020 through a feedback loop in which Cracking the Cryptic videos inspired viewers to build puzzles, which were featured and inspired more constructors ([Nat Alison 2023, 5:17](https://youtu.be/rcIVCrddozQ?t=317)); a large community building on each other's work supplies hundreds of hours of fresh play, the role procedural generation usually plays elsewhere ([Nat Alison 2023, 12:03](https://youtu.be/rcIVCrddozQ?t=723)). Nick McConnell describes the same co-evolution in Angband: players discuss, developers listen and fix, and in the 1990s the game was so extensively modded that many variants appeared and maintainers absorbed pieces back into the main game ([Nick McConnell 2021, 5:44](https://youtu.be/LaOcggk7U88?t=344)).

What communities give people can outweigh the game. Melinda came to ADOM's IRC channel looking for help with its difficulty and stayed for the people and the annual meetups, one of them in Amsterdam where Melinda met ADOM's creator; rarely completing a run, Melinda traces a direct line from dying to jackals in ADOM to a salaried job on Qud ([Ivy Melinda 2020, 10:06](https://youtu.be/db6S2lgTWmI?t=606)). Thomas Biskup, ADOM's creator, recalls a postcard sent around 1996 from war-torn ex-Yugoslavia giving thanks for a game that ran on old computers and gave its player a few hours to think of something other than the war; it taught Biskup the responsibility game makers have to the people they interact with ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 12:56](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=776)). And small communities can carry outsized influence. bhauth argues that traditional roguelikes have few players but disproportionate influence, and that Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup (DCSS) has taken over from NetHack and Angband as the most influential, popular with professional players, streamers and designers; bhauth names Hearthstone's lead designer Mike Donais as holding an octopode win streak ([bhauth 2020, 5:09](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=309)).

**In practice:** treat the community as part of the design. It is where runs become stories, where difficulty gets worked through, and where your game's reputation among other designers is made. The sections that follow are about building for that deliberately.

## Designing for the stories players share: seeds, replays, logs and open data

If stories are what players take away, the game has to make them findable and shareable. The talks give unusually concrete advice here, much of it from fans who had to build the tools themselves.

### Save the data, then make it usable

The most systematic account comes from Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi of SIBR, the fan group that built data tools for Blaseball. Their lessons run in a sequence. First, document where you start: fans documented Blaseball's public API endpoints on GitHub, the developers never asked them to stop, and later tools did not begin from zero. That documentation paid off in the story itself, when fans digging through the API found the ID of the first incinerated player during a vote to bring a player back, kick-starting a major plot event ([Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi 2021, 7:07](https://youtu.be/WeRCGy3-uPY?t=427)). Second, saving data is not enough; it has to be accessible, because a towering stack of raw JSON is no fun to search, and both the people who love JSON and those it terrifies need to find the one needle-in-a-haystack event that makes a story ([Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi 2021, 4:39](https://youtu.be/WeRCGy3-uPY?t=279)). Third, keep raw access even when you offer aggregate statistics, because the questions players ask change over time and unknown unknowns only surface from raw data. SIBR built Datablase to turn raw JSON into indexed game objects queryable by SQL and spreadsheets, then a web API, which supported a hackathon with 58 entries; you do not need a perfect API at the start ([Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi 2021, 7:40](https://youtu.be/WeRCGy3-uPY?t=460)).

Fourth, and the point they weight most heavily: make scrollback easy to view and share. Telling a story requires knowing what happened, not just the result. Blaseball tools posted notable events to Discord, and Reblase made old games searchable as chronological event logs, so fans could pass sequences around and build a shared mythology ([Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi 2021, 15:40](https://youtu.be/WeRCGy3-uPY?t=940)).

> Make viewing scroll back easy, shareable, etc. It is another way to build community by sharing the common seeds of inspiration. — [Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi 2021, 15:40](https://youtu.be/WeRCGy3-uPY?t=940)

Finally, decide what is safe to expose (never personal or login data; SIBR draws a hard line there, and Blaseball's game feed needs no login) and give that to your community, which will do cursed and often blessed things with it ([Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi 2021, 21:26](https://youtu.be/WeRCGy3-uPY?t=1286)). The payoff can come back to the developers: with full data, fans simulated a proposed "double jump" rule against the past season before it went to a vote and published a white paper; the developers later said it had uncovered edge cases they had not anticipated ([Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi 2021, 22:17](https://youtu.be/WeRCGy3-uPY?t=1337)).

For a roguelike, the same speakers point to smaller versions of the idea: Noita's GIF export for sharing funny deaths, and the wish that strategy games kept a full, filterable game log that could be read as a story ([Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi 2021, 19:33](https://youtu.be/WeRCGy3-uPY?t=1173)).

### Design at the scale players share

Mike Cook supplies the reason those small tools matter. At what Cook calls the "lens" scale, players share one cropped thing: a screenshot, a short clip, a single object. A Minecraft seed describes a world larger than Earth, but people pass it on for one specific thing near spawn; Dwarf Fortress stories are complex but usually start from one cropped detail such as a dwarf's description. So examine your generator's output at that scale too, not only as whole maps or whole runs ([Mike Cook 2026, 22:02](https://youtu.be/nOGNdrjm8ek?t=1322)).

The genre already has tools built for this scale. DCSS saves a morgue file, a text snapshot of the character and key events, for every online game, and players can generate one mid-game; Alan Malloy explains that a community norm of attaching a morgue to any help request makes those requests answerable, because the morgue usually reveals a string of basic mistakes rather than the single problem the player suspected ([Alan Malloy 2017, 9:35](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=575)). Caves of Qud lets players type in a world seed, so stream viewers can play largely the same generated world as the developers on screen; the developers say it "sort of works", since most of the world matches, and that entering the same seed is itself a shared experience ([Jason Grinblat et al. 2018, 10:15](https://youtu.be/owmGknfj6H4?t=615)). Melinda describes Qud's Discord "build club", which ran for a few months after the procedurally generated villages update: anyone could post a character code, seed and starting village, different players took characters from the same start in different directions, and the club produced fan art and exposed world-seeding bugs ([Ivy Melinda 2020, 20:07](https://youtu.be/db6S2lgTWmI?t=1207)).

The gap shows when the tools are missing. Gabriel Koenig's Test Tube Titans let players breed unique procedural creatures, some of which Koenig had never seen, but they could share them only by exporting files or taking screenshots, with no in-game way to show them off ([Gabriel Koenig 2020, 20:55](https://youtu.be/xju91VGh2Ps?t=1255)).

### Shared mystery and live response

Shared data supports a second kind of collective play: speculation. Alexei Pepers describes how Blaseball, where all players shared one simulation, let fans vote on mysterious rule-changing decrees of which only one passed. In season 10 "black hole" passed and was revealed; "countdown self-destruct" never passed and remains unknown, a permanent object of debate ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 28:47](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=1727)). Clark adds that the developers reacted alongside players: when randomness shook out in surprising ways, or the community rallied around something such as a team with no pitchers, they changed course and ran with it, making each season a dialogue between developers and community ([Joel Clark 2020, 12:21](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=741)). That openness extended to keeping known flaws. Asked whether the blessing vote let large fan blocs gain outsized power, Clark agreed: it was designed as a raffle, it is a broken system they are leaving in, and they patch around it with new systems such as a differently balanced "enhanced party time" ([Joel Clark 2020, 32:01](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=1921)). Florence Smith Nicholls cites Necrocracy, a live game with a bespoke conspiracy-board tool where players mapped their theories, which then informed each week's live design ([Florence Smith Nicholls 2023, 7:56](https://youtu.be/MQw3pe-z6JM?t=476)).

The desire for shared discovery can even outweigh procedural generation. Slashie's newest project, an exploration-only forest game, sets aside some of its procedural generation for a large, non-procedural world precisely so players can share their findings socially, and keeps its discoveries strange and unexplained so players form their own hypotheses ([slashie 2026, 9:12:22](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=33142)). That is a real trade-off: a unique world per player makes every story personal, a common world makes every discovery comparable.

### Show the generator itself

The generator can be something to share as well. bleeptrack hands out generative stickers like business cards; telling people that every sticker on the table is unique makes them spend minutes choosing the one that suits them ([bleeptrack 2025, 5:45](https://youtu.be/FWQwtn-46rs?t=345)). bleeptrack also brings pen plotters to events, where live drawing draws people in and starts conversations, and people value the result more because they can see the machine's effort ([bleeptrack 2025, 13:50](https://youtu.be/FWQwtn-46rs?t=830)). Darius Kazemi urges developers to publish interactive deconstructions of their own level generators, which is easier than writing an essay or giving a talk and, especially for browser games, more useful to others; several roguelike authors told Kazemi they based their level generation entirely on Kazemi's Spelunky toy ([Darius Kazemi 2017, 14:49](https://youtu.be/CLi4PWxDmAI?t=889)).

**In practice:** build export, logs, seeds and a safe public data feed in from the start, rather than leaving fans to reverse-engineer them. Make the smallest shareable unit (a death GIF, a morgue, a seed, a single creature) one action away.

## Playing together online: servers, spectating, scores and competition

Putting a single-player roguelike online need not change a single rule, yet it changes how the game is learned and played. Two talks about the genre's public servers make this case independently.

### What a server gives a single-player game

Alan Malloy argues that DCSS's online play, offered alongside the downloadable game, brings benefits many other roguelikes could have: it reaches more players, collects game data for analysis without spyware-like agents, and creates a social space, events and better feedback, all of which ultimately make the game better for players ([Alan Malloy 2017, 0:30](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=30)). Drew Streib, who ran the public NetHack server NAO (nethack.alt.org), makes the narrower and striking claim that live game watching does not change NetHack but accelerates the learning curve so much that players who once took years to ascend (win) now often do it within weeks. Players at first objected that their secrets were being given away, so NAO shows a banner saying all games are watched; Streib calls ttyrec (terminal recording) watching a "prehistoric Twitch" ([Drew Streib 2016, 11:44](https://youtu.be/J4RK-3zW8vY?t=704)).

> It doesn't change the game, it just accelerates the learning curve. — [Drew Streib 2016, 11:44](https://youtu.be/J4RK-3zW8vY?t=704)

The mechanisms behind that acceleration are specific:

- **Live mentoring.** An event organiser in Streib's audience described ascending on NAO while IRC helpers watched the game and said exactly what to do, and a friend sent advice by in-game mail; Streib calls it a more advanced spoiler and is fine with it ([Drew Streib 2016, 28:59](https://youtu.be/J4RK-3zW8vY?t=1739)).
- **Weightless mail.** NAO's in-game mail is delivered by a mail daemon, and the letters weigh nothing and evaporate after reading so they cannot become extra items; NAO also records ttyrec replays of every game ([Adeon 2017, 1:33:43](https://youtu.be/rIB0y_kwFuY?t=5623)).
- **Cross-mode spectating and scorekeeping.** In DCSS anyone can spectate any online game in console or tiles regardless of how it is being played, so a console-only helper can read a tiles player's problem, and scorekeeping pages show per-player combos, streaks, win rates and high scores without queries, giving players ways to brag and get help ([Alan Malloy 2017, 20:54](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=1254)).
- **Shared bones.** NetHack's bones files (a dead character's level, left for a later player to find) only become a real part of the game on a shared server; Streib says stumbling on someone else's bones was their only realistic chance to ascend, and felt less like cheating than inserting a level themselves ([Drew Streib 2016, 5:33](https://youtu.be/J4RK-3zW8vY?t=333)).
- **Comparable challenges.** Biskup launched ADOM's Rogue League server with global high scores because challenge modes only make sense when players can compare results, not just discuss them on a forum ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 3:40](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=220)).
- **Group events.** Russ described a university NetHack server built for 12-24 hour group binges: a live "binge board" projected on the wall, player stats written to a database that granted cross-game achievements, and a Twitter bot announcing deaths ([Tariq et al. 2016, 10:55](https://youtu.be/SDojcmObQzw?t=655)).

### What scores have to mean

Once results are shared, fairness becomes a design concern. The Rogue panel recalls that a shared high-score file changed Rogue's priorities: cheating for your own fun is fine, but competing against others made fairness and save-file security matter, and Ken Thompson reportedly cheated by copying save files and replaying ([Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 20:56](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=1256)). Streib ran a server mainly to prove personal achievements, and NAO takes a hard line against restoring games so that a score on it means something. Yet Streib also warns that fewer people care about your bragging rights than you think ([Drew Streib 2016, 6:37](https://youtu.be/J4RK-3zW8vY?t=397)). Both are true: verification matters to the competitive minority, and you should not build the whole service around it.

Patches complicate scores. Jim Shepard calls wiping leaderboards on big patches, as Diablo's seasonal ladder does, the "nuclear option", and fair: if a patch accidentally made something too strong, that is the developer's mistake, so give the previous champion a special powerless hat and start over ([Jim Shepard 2017, 29:09](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=1749)).

Tournaments can also push players toward variety. Malloy describes DCSS's automated release tournaments: for about two weeks after each release every online game counts; popular easy combos such as Minotaur Berserker of Trog award fewer points as they are won, and a rotating rarely played combo pays big bonuses to its first eight winners. Malloy's own feeling is that the scoring rewards playing a lot more than playing well ([Alan Malloy 2017, 28:41](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=1721)). Kawa singles out that randomised combo challenge as a personal favourite conduct-like goal, combinations "no sane person" would pick ([Kawa 2019, 21:35](https://youtu.be/KLHJsJuJfYg?t=1295)). Angband has run an ongoing competition judged by turn count for a long time, which is why McConnell says speedrunners did not change the game much ([Nick McConnell 2021, 14:22](https://youtu.be/LaOcggk7U88?t=862)).

### Speedruns and play out of bounds

Speedrunning is the extreme of public play. Adeon's NetHack real-time record of about one hour three minutes took roughly a month and around 1,000 attempts, so a live run has to balance risk against a realistic chance to win; Adeon put the odds at about 30 percent in a two-hour slot and finished in about 1:50, against commentators' first wins of 20 to 36 hours ([Adeon 2017, 0:18](https://youtu.be/rIB0y_kwFuY?t=18)). Everest Pipkin describes how speedrunners stop seeing a level as platforms and walls and start seeing pockets of inside and outside, turning clipping into memorised routes ([Everest Pipkin 2023, 22:53](https://youtu.be/O78uYtUZKYs?t=1373)), and how the same out-of-bounds play becomes social space: teenage parties held beneath World of Warcraft's maps, reached by known routes, with rules like "there will not be fighting here" layered on top by the players ([Everest Pipkin 2023, 21:13](https://youtu.be/O78uYtUZKYs?t=1273)).

### Convenience against togetherness, and an edge case

Online structure involves trade-offs. Gavin Verhey explains that Magic Online's pod drafts could take 50 minutes to three hours, with forced idling if your match ended early, so Magic Arena paired players from a large pool to allow drafting at 2 a.m., trading the shared-pod feel for convenience, a trade Verhey considers well worth it ([Gavin Verhey 2024, 22:50](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=1370)). And "online" stretches further than you might expect: Leif Bloomquist builds multiplayer roguelikes for the Commodore 64, which suits the project because it is exhaustively documented after decades of reverse engineering, has an active community and huge library (around 25,000 games, many of them roguelikes), and now has network adapters that put it on the internet ([Leif Bloomquist 2019, 1:48](https://youtu.be/ASGn5J9PHbs?t=108); [Leif Bloomquist 2020, 3:01](https://youtu.be/bpSnPNr6ETc?t=181)).

**In practice:** treat online infrastructure first as a learning and social tool: spectating, replays, shared bones, scoreboards. Decide early what a score must prove and what a balance patch does to existing records.

## Modding and fan reinterpretation

Opening a roguelike's data turns some players into co-authors, and the talks agree that this grows the community around the game.

### Reinterpretation and why it builds community

Ray, from the Caves of Qud wiki team, gives the framing: modular data files give players a strong capacity for reinterpretation, which Ray defines as the ability to parse, reuse and transform a game's data, whether for a wiki or for a mod ([Ray 2023, 4:15](https://youtu.be/n6mKigS_71Y?t=255)). Several developers converge on the community payoff. Josh Ge says you need a community to have a successful roguelike, and that giving players tools to build their own content for Ge's X-COM roguelike helped build one ([Josh Ge 2016, 6:48](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=408)). Benjamin Berman points to Pokemon Showdown, which sustains around 15,000 concurrent players on community-authored content with around 17,000 commits; Berman's advice is simply to do what players ask for ([Benjamin Berman 2019, 19:05](https://youtu.be/DT9_7sW5knY?t=1145)). Dylan Gedig found that streamers' audiences supplied Peglin with modders, translators and a wiki even though the game was not built to be modded, and the mods produced more content for streamers than two developers could ([Dylan Gedig 2022, 13:14](https://youtu.be/ke0cLTVg2_M?t=794)).

### How to make a game moddable

The technical advice is consistent: keep content in data.

- **Offer more than one way in.** George Moromisato argues that pairing data files with scripting widens the modding community beyond programmers to people contributing flavour text and graphics; Dwarf Fortress, Caves of Qud and Moromisato's own Transcendence all offer several routes ([George Moromisato 2022, 18:31](https://youtu.be/mES03vaZo3U?t=1111)).
- **Prefer data files where you can.** Ray finds data-file mods significantly more robust to game and interface changes than pure scripting; a favourite mod changes one property of an item in three or four lines of XML, and modders can recombine existing parts ([Ray 2023, 7:58](https://youtu.be/n6mKigS_71Y?t=478)).
- **Get modding as a side effect of architecture.** Biskup explains that because Ultimate ADOM's engine interprets configuration, modding comes almost free; Biskup offers opening it, first internally and then to the community, as a compromise in the debate over open-sourcing ADOM (the reasons for keeping the source closed are in the chapter's last section), and imagines a Rogue League area where mods are listed, rated and discussed ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 17:29](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=1049)). The same setup allows optional content modules, such as a time-travel extension, that do not clutter the main game but are there for players who want them ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 26:18](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=1578)).
- **Keep logic in accessible files.** Kate Compton recalls that The Sims stored much of its UI and AI in external files, so players hacked and re-uploaded tiny programs at a time when editing a program on the fly was hard ([Kate Compton 2020, 6:46](https://youtu.be/E5-3Ui7oO8U?t=406)).
- **Make swappable functions modular too.** Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang describe Qud's language packages as mods that replace "replacer" functions one for one: number-to-word conversion has to be procedural, and Turkish writes "May 5" rather than "May 5th", so the Turkish package simply supplies its own replacer ([Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang 2026, 1:52:03](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=6723)). That work covers over 20,000 strings and about 150,000 words, and community translations into other languages already appear as Workshop mods on a public experimental branch ([Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang 2026, 1:55:10](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=6910)).

### Leave room and treat modders as colleagues

Moromisato's craft advice is to leave deliberate "whitespace". Transcendence implements only the central areas of its map, leaving other regions to modders, perhaps with a hint like "the pirate realm", and skips some item tiers (a Mark IV or VI) so players imagine and build them ([George Moromisato 2022, 21:49](https://youtu.be/mES03vaZo3U?t=1309)). Moromisato also urges treating modders as equal co-developers and sharing as much as possible, including setting and character background, so their content fits; Bucklew told Moromisato Caves of Qud hired one of its modders ([George Moromisato 2022, 22:51](https://youtu.be/mES03vaZo3U?t=1371)).

### When fan work becomes the game

That is not an isolated case. Qud's hindren began as Caelyn Sandel's fan creation; the writing captured the game's voice so well that Sandel was hired and added them to the game, which Melinda calls the community leapfrogging from fan work to canon ([Ivy Melinda 2020, 16:52](https://youtu.be/db6S2lgTWmI?t=1012)). Crypt of the NecroDancer's Synchrony DLC began when Adrian Zeyfang read the developers saying online multiplayer was impossible, took it as a challenge, and built a fan prototype with friends over months and years until the studio adopted it ([Adrian Zeyfang 2024, 1:10](https://youtu.be/zwhNSbFVKQM?t=70)). Berman credits Slay the Spire with embracing mods, so players could edit the Java game to add cards and show what they wanted without asking permission ([Benjamin Berman 2019, 10:19](https://youtu.be/DT9_7sW5knY?t=619)). Mods can also extend a game toward what its community values: a fan homesteading mod for Qud adds diegetic building, which Melinda feels makes the game more honest by letting players build a home where community gathers ([Ivy Melinda 2020, 21:07](https://youtu.be/db6S2lgTWmI?t=1267)). And player-made challenges are a lighter form of the same thing: Philomena Schwab says Niche's custom difficulty settings let players design and share challenges and custom characters for role-play, which kept the game alive for years without updates ([Philomena Schwab 2022, 8:46](https://youtu.be/wLLDPz8PnQg?t=526)).

### Wikis, companions and source code

Reinterpretation also means reference tools. The Qud wiki parses the game's data files and uploads object blueprints automatically into MediaWiki cargo tables, with a blueprint explorer flagging pages that need updates, so content stays current and items can be searched and filtered like a database ([Ray 2023, 4:37](https://youtu.be/n6mKigS_71Y?t=277)). Ray's warning is that a game's ontology is not a wiki's: three doors needing three keys are separate objects in Qud, but should each have its own page? The wiki team keeps a sheet of overrides and writes prose that cannot be generated ([Ray 2023, 6:13](https://youtu.be/n6mKigS_71Y?t=373)). Jeremy Rose built a Cataclysm companion guide as a static web app that downloads a version's data once (about 3.5 MB of gzipped JSON) and then works offline, with crowdsourced translations in the same 10 languages as the game ([Jeremy Rose 2022, 14:52](https://youtu.be/ziN33iMQVPo?t=892)). Open source opens the deepest layer: Alexei Pepers urges developers to read the source of their favourite open-source roguelikes, since NetHack is on git and its wiki's footnotes link straight into source files, and the comments alone teach technique and design reasoning ([Alexei Pepers 2018, 23:28](https://youtu.be/5y_IAdOwaYs?t=1408)).

### How close to stand

Developers disagree about how close to get. Subset Games, surprised by how much players modded FTL, made Into the Breach easier to mod through scripting and tries not to break mods with updates, though they lack time to build full tools; Matthew Davis calls fans continuing to play with your ideas nothing but a compliment ([Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 23:58](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=1438)). Jon Perry, by contrast, keeps UFO 50 mods at arm's length and does not look closely at them, so they cannot influence Perry on any return to those systems; the host adds that creators engaging too closely can turn a fan scene into a contest for approval ([Jon Perry 2025, 31:04](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=1864)). Qud sits at the other end, hiring modders and fan writers. The choice depends on whether you want fan work to shape your own design or to run in parallel with it.

**In practice:** keep content in data files, document the formats, leave visible gaps worth filling, avoid breaking mods casually, and decide deliberately how much of what modders make you will look at.

## Developing in the open: releasing early and showing you listen

Roguelikes are unusually well suited to open development, because the same players replay the game after every change and can tell you what each one did.

### The case and the history

Chris King, who spent nine or ten years on 20XX and 30XX, makes this argument directly: roguelike players naturally replay, so when you develop in the open the same audience responds to each change and keeps giving feedback as the design evolves. Community input was a critical part of King's iteration, and both games stayed in Steam Early Access much longer than planned ([Chris King 2022, 1:00](https://youtu.be/1Np1DSdpoR0?t=60)).

> We have a natural audience that wants to play and replay our games. — [Chris King 2022, 1:00](https://youtu.be/1Np1DSdpoR0?t=60)

The genre's history bears this out, including its uncomfortable start. ADOM's first public release, posted to Usenet in early 1996 after two years of work, got no reaction at all; Biskup kept going only out of personal enjoyment of the game, and a month later 0.7.1 brought the first few dozen emails ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 6:15](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=375)). After that, monthly releases built a fast-growing loop: by 0.8.0 hundreds of emails had arrived from players in places like the US and Finland, a feedback loop Biskup describes as being like a drug that pushed development ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 6:55](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=415)). Decades later Slay the Spire's two years of early access with constant feedback honed the card-roguelike interface, Berman says ([Benjamin Berman 2019, 10:19](https://youtu.be/DT9_7sW5knY?t=619)).

### Release early and often

The practical advice converges. Josh Ge calls "release early and often" the roguelike developer's mantra: get the game minimally playable quickly, post in weekly threads such as r/roguelikedev's Sharing Saturday (useful for accountability and community even in a week with little progress), and keep a public dev blog that concentrates information in one place ([Josh Ge 2018, 25:15](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=1515)). Santiago Zapata treats player feedback as the most important metric for judging what worked, and the 7DRL (Seven Day Roguelike Challenge), with its 200-plus entries and attention, as a good source of it ([Santiago Zapata 2016, 26:12](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=1572)). Zapata also found that setting small learning games in established universes such as Zelda, Metroid or Castlevania drew players in and brought the feedback a learning developer needs ([Santiago Zapata 2016, 8:46](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=526)). Evan Debenham publishes about a dozen blog posts a year on Shattered Pixel Dungeon's plans, which excites players, forces ideas to be made concrete and gathers feedback on content before it ships ([Evan Debenham 2021, 17:49](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=1069)). Nick McConnell says discussion and playtesting on Angband's forums have massively improved many design ideas, McConnell's own and others' ([Nick McConnell 2021, 11:38](https://youtu.be/LaOcggk7U88?t=698)). Andrea Roberts's team took Roundguard to public indie show-and-tell events in Seattle from the first months, watching strangers, including children, play over their shoulders ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 29:23](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=1763)).

Ge also warns from experience against the opposite. Years spent avoiding social media and community discussion were, by Ge's own account, a mistake that slowed things down: the varied opinions about roguelikes are more than you can think of yourself ([Josh Ge 2016, 12:43](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=763)). And others can steer you round your particular pitfalls only if you ask; Ge points newcomers to r/roguelikedev, its tutorials and summer code-along, FAQ Fridays, the Discord, RogueBasin and Roguelike Radio ([Josh Ge 2018, 12:32](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=752)).

### Lower the friction, close the loop

Two techniques make open development pay. The first is making feedback effortless. King puts buttons linking to forums and Discord in the game, and points to Rogue Legacy 2's F10 key, which opens a report form that attaches diagnostic information; asking players to DM or email you wastes your time and theirs ([Chris King 2022, 4:35](https://youtu.be/1Np1DSdpoR0?t=275)).

The second is showing that you listened. Players give more feedback when they see it acted on, so King posts in public, chats in Discord and writes verbose patch notes that credit community-suggested changes; being civil and professional without being uptight sets a tone others follow ([Chris King 2022, 6:22](https://youtu.be/1Np1DSdpoR0?t=382)). Brian Cronin, a solo part-time developer, finds that playtesting doubles as community building: the Discord for Cronin's game is almost entirely past playtesters ([Brian Cronin 2025, 8:38](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=518)). Cronin attributes each action item to the tester who raised it and sends a follow-up note once it is acted on, which thanks them, builds trust and makes them keen to test again ([Brian Cronin 2025, 26:33](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=1593)).

**In practice:** ship small and often, put the feedback channel one click or one key away, and visibly credit what you act on.

## Reading feedback: desires, complaints and the silent majority

Collecting feedback is the easy part. The talks spend more time on how to interpret it.

### Valid information, not instructions

Several developers converge on the same stance: everything players say is real information about their experience, and none of it is a specification. Debenham says the main value of feedback is perspective, keeping a solo developer from becoming an echo chamber building only what they like, though dedicated players can be the most biased; biased feedback is not worthless, but you must recognise and account for the bias ([Evan Debenham 2021, 10:58](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=658)). Debenham's method is to look for the desire behind a suggestion. Players have repeatedly and seriously asked for Sans from Undertale as a Shattered Pixel Dungeon boss; the request is absurd, but the desire for more interesting boss fights is real and can be met ([Evan Debenham 2021, 11:42](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=702)).

Subset Games' Justin Ma and Matthew Davis treat every complaint as valid, then diagnose it: is it a design issue, a presentation issue, or players wanting a different game? Then find a middle ground or explain your reasoning, as they did after repeated criticism of Into the Breach's weapon costs and shop, sticking to what their testing supported ([Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 9:37](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=577)). The Against the Storm developers, Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński, put the burden squarely on the designer: players have every right to give emotional or wrong feedback, and unpacking it is the designer's job ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 19:48](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=1188)). One common misreading they warn against: requests to buff something often mean it is someone's favourite playstyle, not that it is weak, and player-proposed fixes often miss the real problem; a "weak perk" on their upvote board may really be a playstyle that is not yet well defined ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 16:58](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=1018)). Cole Wehrle grounds the same stance in reader-response theory: a player sees only a slice of the game, the designer is not every player, so even a very negative experience is valid information, and Wehrle reads every comment that can be found ([Cole Wehrle 2025, 5:48](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=348)).

> Every experience of playing a game, even a really negative one, is a kind of valid experience. — [Cole Wehrle 2025, 5:48](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=348)

### The people who are not talking

The loudest feedback comes from the unhappy. Erik Osheim and Robert Au, maintaining Angband, heard most from veterans who disliked changes, some of whom forked variants or said the game had got too easy; without polling data, vocal critics dominate, yet a silent majority enjoyed the changes and some critics came round. They did act where the complaint held up, running simulations that showed item distribution had risen, and adjusting it ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 25:51](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=1551)). DiIorio states the rule: if you change the game to appeal to vocal critics, take the quiet, content players into account, or the two groups simply swap places and you end up playing feedback whack-a-mole ([Dan DiIorio 2025, 3:10](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=190)). Tyler Coleman offers a way to read silence: about 20% of a game's content drives 80% of the conversation, and the familiar foundation (controls, camera, key mapping) should be quiet, because when people talk about it, it is rarely good ([Tyler Coleman 2024, 21:14](https://youtu.be/C6jR41fZjqM?t=1274)).

Timing helps separate a bad change from an unfamiliar one. Against the Storm's developers wait about two weeks before reacting to backlash, because players often adapt and find a niche for the change; by then they can tell a productive disruption from universally hated design, and team members with different temperaments plus a player-focused community manager balance the urge to react ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 21:22](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=1282)). Debenham adds a test: when veterans object, check whether they give actionable reasons for disliking the new thing or simply want it changed back. Some reflexive resistance, as when Debenham remade Shattered's decade-old music, is unavoidable and has to be accepted ([Evan Debenham 2021, 27:24](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=1644)).

### Sources beyond the comment box

Comments are not the only channel. Sandel watched people stream Caves of Qud on Twitch to find where new players got confused and frustrated, which Sandel found very useful for outreach ([Caelyn Sandel 2020, 15:49](https://youtu.be/NANqgqeqh2k?t=949)). Schwab's team surveyed 6,000 beta testers of The Wandering Village and found that nearly everyone rating it 7 or below found it too hard, a split no single balance could fix, which led them to difficulty settings ([Philomena Schwab 2022, 9:59](https://youtu.be/wLLDPz8PnQg?t=599)). Debenham gathers from email, community channels and app store reviews ([Evan Debenham 2021, 10:58](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=658)).

### Special cases

Some feedback shifts as a community matures. Shawn Main observes that the longer a community spends with a game, the better it identifies where overt randomness decides wins and losses, and the more it demands reward for skill ([Shawn Main 2017, 12:18](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=738)). Hybrid games face two audiences at once: Jonathan Lessard reports that chess players gave Chogue harsh feedback for leaving out castling and en passant, rules the designers had dropped through laziness or never thought of, and Pippin Barr insisted on a resign option because chess players expect one ([Jonathan Lessard 2018, 29:36](https://youtu.be/l1YEJBKehAY?t=1776)).

**In practice:** collect widely, including streams and surveys; diagnose each complaint before acting; wait before reversing a change; and weigh the players who are not talking.

## Tending the space: care, moderation, volunteers and limits

A healthy community does not form by itself, and keeping it healthy costs real time.

### Cultivate it or someone else will

Ivy Melinda, who watched the Caves of Qud Discord grow from half a dozen people to over 3,000, says "management" oversells the role, which is care and cultivation, and that there is no one-size-fits-all recipe ([Ivy Melinda 2020, 0:54](https://youtu.be/db6S2lgTWmI?t=54)). Caelyn Sandel gives the reason it cannot be left alone: if a community forms itself, the loudest and meanest voices end up running it, and hostile elements take over unless shown the door. Qud's team instead built a space for people pushed out of other gaming spaces, consistent with the game's values of bodily autonomy and anti-authoritarianism ([Caelyn Sandel 2020, 22:15](https://youtu.be/NANqgqeqh2k?t=1335)). Sandel closes with questions every developer should ask: what is it like to be a new player here, who feels welcome or alienated, and who is guiding your game's online presence if you are not ([Caelyn Sandel 2020, 23:57](https://youtu.be/NANqgqeqh2k?t=1437)).

> If you are not guiding your games online presence, who is? Because someone will. — [Caelyn Sandel 2020, 23:57](https://youtu.be/NANqgqeqh2k?t=1437)

### Structures that spread the work

As Qud's community grew, it added an official wiki with a volunteer crew, volunteer moderators called "mayors", a Patreon and a subreddit; Melinda, too, started as a moderator of a handful of people and later received a stipend ([Ivy Melinda 2020, 14:57](https://youtu.be/db6S2lgTWmI?t=897)). Asked about relying on volunteers in a commercial project, Melinda says it is opt-in, many people want to give back but do not know how, and offering them ways to do so benefits them, the community and the developer ([Ivy Melinda 2020, 23:58](https://youtu.be/db6S2lgTWmI?t=1438)). Players can build institutions on their own: Nicholas Feinberg describes DCSS's learndb, a player-curated knowledge base of over 10,000 entries that includes drama, vanity entries and a curated list of thousands of rejected player suggestions, such as scurvy for not eating fruit ([Nicholas Feinberg 2020, 1:06](https://youtu.be/GMkBT4UbvAs?t=66)). Chris King's force multiplier is to answer questions in public, persistent places, so veterans absorb the answers and give them to newcomers for you ([Chris King 2022, 8:11](https://youtu.be/1Np1DSdpoR0?t=491)).

### Costs and limits

The work is real. King spent about 8 hours a week, 15-16% of working time, on community interaction for 20XX, and learned only after not planning for it the first time that encouraging feedback without a sustainable process leads to burnout: plan the time, be present at patches and releases, and batch the work into quiet periods ([Chris King 2022, 13:42](https://youtu.be/1Np1DSdpoR0?t=822)). Inviting players into the content adds more. Elliot Trinidad reports that Blaseball's user-submitted names, a Patreon perk, built buy-in but required heavy moderation of unsavoury, borderline and copyright-infringing names, and drifted the world's tone toward bombastic names ([Elliot Trinidad 2023, 10:12](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=612)).

Growth brings expectations. Biskup calls ADOM's community in its "boomtown" years awesome and full of ideas, but a larger audience brought expectations, and the self-imposed deadlines that went unmet became a defining lesson of that period ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 7:51](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=471)). Absence costs trust: reviving ADOM after years of little contact meant slowly rekindling both Biskup's own passion and players' belief that something would really happen; releasing JADE in 2011 helped by showing something tangible ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 17:42](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=1062)).

There is also a personal limit for the people doing the tending. Melinda avoids heavy mod use so that personal play stays close to an entry-level experience, since heavily modded Qud can become unrecognisable and guiding new players requires knowing what they face ([Ivy Melinda 2020, 24:50](https://youtu.be/db6S2lgTWmI?t=1490)).

**In practice:** budget community time as part of development, set the tone early and enforce it, answer in public, and give invested players defined, optional ways to help.

## Who the game is for: niche depth, wider audiences and newcomers

The sections so far assume the players are already there. The rest of the chapter turns to the business that depends on them: who the game is for, how it gets found, how it pays, and who owns what a community makes.

Every commercial roguelike faces the same fork early: build for the people who already love the genre and want to think hard, or reach for players who have never heard the word "roguelike". The talks do not agree on which road is right.

### The case for staying a niche

The creators of Rogue were relaxed about the niche. On the 2016 Rogue panel, Glenn Wichman described roguelikes as games for people who want something hard rather than twitchy, and another panelist noted that Rogue was sold in boxes and never reached a mass market: that ship has sailed, and that is fine ([Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 18:17](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=1097)).

> You can make something that has quality that's inherent, that's beautiful, that doesn't appeal to everybody. — [Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 18:17](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=1097)

David Brevik adds that the conditions for a niche have improved since 1994: streaming, YouTube and Discord give developers direct access to a huge gaming audience, so a niche game can succeed even when its audience is nowhere near AAA size ([David Brevik 2023, 27:13](https://youtu.be/OwFrTY3IoQQ?t=1633)). Scott Burger's Steam data suggests the niche is a loyal one. Comparing playtime recorded at review, the median for all rogue-style games is about 20 hours against 31 for games tagged traditional roguelike, about 40% longer; at the 90th percentile the gap is about 137 hours against 300 ([Scott Burger 2023, 29:13](https://youtu.be/IliQZm5Itng?t=1753)). Players who choose the traditional form stay with it.

### The case for reaching wider

Thomas Biskup argues the other side most forcefully. In Biskup's view the "ugly truth" is that traditional roguelikes are not successful in the mainstream, even though RogueBasin and Steam list more of them than ever; mainstream hits combine great design, a great user interface and a large community, and of the three, design is the cheapest ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 2:06](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=126)). The team believes there is still room in the mainstream for highly detailed roguelikes, and notes that mainstream games keep adopting roguelike patterns without accepting roguelikes themselves ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 4:22](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=262)). Ultimate ADOM was the result: an attempt to reach a wider, more casual audience without sacrificing complexity, partly because a commercial game needs more players to earn money, which is also why it dropped ASCII-only graphics ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 1:48](https://youtu.be/PTIsUSbQ0TA?t=108)).

Biskup frames the decision as binary. A game aimed at the roguelike community can keep 30-year-old conventions; a game aimed wider has to forget the genre's assumptions, rethink everything, and only then work out how to accommodate the existing community, which takes bravery and may mean doing things that community initially dislikes ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 20:44](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1244)).

Josh Ge names a narrower lever. Ge argues roguelikes reach wider audiences mainly through polish, which most traditional roguelikes lack and polished roguelites have; Cogmind was built by perfecting each feature before moving on, which is why, Ge says, it took so long ([Josh Ge 2016, 15:57](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=957)). Ge reports a payoff, with several players saying Cogmind was the first non-roguelite roguelike they played after many roguelites, and hopes other developers adopt the same features so players can keep going into the genre ([Josh Ge 2016, 28:45](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1725)). A polished traditional game can be a bridge rather than a compromise.

What the choice depends on is mostly money and intent. The panel's and Brevik's position suits a developer who can live on a small, loyal audience; Biskup's suits a team that has to pay salaries. Ge's suggests the two are less opposed than they look, since a polished traditional game can carry new players into the genre rather than away from it ([Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 18:17](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=1097); [David Brevik 2023, 27:13](https://youtu.be/OwFrTY3IoQQ?t=1633); [Thomas Biskup 2018, 1:48](https://youtu.be/PTIsUSbQ0TA?t=108); [Josh Ge 2016, 28:45](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1725)).

### Designing for specific new audiences

Several talks pick a particular audience outside the core and ask what it needs.

- **Time-poor adults.** Andrea Roberts found, as a new parent, that a roguelike offered real strategic depth in 35-45 minute sessions that could be picked up a week later without resuming an epic storyline or sorting an inventory mess; the clean fresh start is the feature ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 2:22](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=142)). Roberts also heard from parents that their children enjoyed the repetition, practice and learning, and connects that to values the genre spreads: exploration, comfort in failure, grit ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 2:22](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=142)).
- **Children.** Michael Langford argues roguelikes suit young children because they offer a lot of replayable content at a single skill level, unlike "one and done" games such as Mario, and that small accessibility changes open up parents' large spending on children, especially on non-PC platforms ([Michael Langford 2021, 2:20](https://youtu.be/wPN5bPxWXm8?t=140)). Langford's tool is the "shame test": imagine playing within earshot of a child you barely know (in the example given, a friend's husband's boss's child), screenshot every moment you would feel embarrassed, and put those gross sounds, graphic art or deceptive content behind toggles so parents can let children play; the art should still express the full range of emotions ([Michael Langford 2021, 13:00](https://youtu.be/wPN5bPxWXm8?t=780)).
- **Players who judge by the art.** Philomena Schwab warns that a cute, colourful style signals an easy, casual game. Darkest Dungeon and Dark Souls pre-select teenage and older players through dark settings and complex UI, while Niche, just as complex as Darkest Dungeon, drew many young girls who wanted to play with animals alongside adults who wanted depth, and catering to both was hard ([Philomena Schwab 2022, 5:28](https://youtu.be/wLLDPz8PnQg?t=328)). Your art chooses an audience whether you mean it to or not.
- **Players who come for a brand.** John Harris notes that Pokemon Mystery Dungeon's Explorers games sold about 6 million, far beyond Shiren 5 and 6 at around 200,000, and that many people who have never heard of roguelikes enjoyed it through the power of the brand ([John Harris 2024, 9:57](https://youtu.be/0MdNwIHwXy0?t=597)).

### Newcomers and the core are not enemies

Wider reach provokes resistance from the existing community. Caelyn Sandel argues that the needs of core and new players are not actually at odds, even though core communities often see accessibility options as pandering: new players need a welcoming introduction, core players need to stay interested, and the developer's job is to balance both and to convince the core that this is possible ([Caelyn Sandel 2020, 20:43](https://youtu.be/NANqgqeqh2k?t=1243)). Drew Streib reached the same conclusion from running a NetHack server. Streib admits to having once rolled their eyes at the Reddit NetHack crowd, but now argues a community stays alive only by broadening access, through browser and phone play for example, because a big audience fills the pipeline of new players ([Drew Streib 2016, 27:14](https://youtu.be/J4RK-3zW8vY?t=1634)).

Some games have no obvious audience at all. At the 2018 lightning talks a developer showed a contemplative procedural game about observing and photographing generated alien whale pods, comparing flukes and dorsal fins, and admitted to having no idea who it was for or where to find them ([Various 2018, 41:15](https://youtu.be/60MTG-__dt4?t=2475)). Nobody in the talks offers a general answer.

**In practice:** decide who your main audience is before you commit to art, interface and onboarding. If it is the existing roguelike community, you can lean on its conventions. If it is wider, budget for polish, check what your art promises, run something like Langford's shame test if children or families are in view, and plan how you will bring the core along ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 20:44](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1244); [Philomena Schwab 2022, 5:28](https://youtu.be/wLLDPz8PnQg?t=328); [Caelyn Sandel 2020, 20:43](https://youtu.be/NANqgqeqh2k?t=1243)).

## Standing out in a crowded market: genre signals, tags and niches

A roguelike released today competes with thousands. Scott Burger's Steam dataset counts about 7,870 rogue-style games across six tags: roughly 6,000 tagged roguelike, 4,000-5,000 roguelite and 3,700 action roguelike, then a drop to about 400 roguelike deckbuilders, 326 traditional roguelikes and 475 roguevanias, with many games carrying several tags ([Scott Burger 2023, 12:50](https://youtu.be/IliQZm5Itng?t=770)). David Dunham found 2,554 games under Steam's roguelike deckbuilder tag in 2026, up about 700 in the months between proposing the talk and giving it ([David Dunham 2026, 11:07](https://youtu.be/oipNr8RE5bA?t=667)). In a field that size, the first problem is being read correctly, and the second is being found at all.

### What your screenshots promise

Players read genre from a glance. Dunham's publisher, Kitfox, warned that a game whose screenshots show cards will be read as a roguelike deckbuilder or card battler, which disappoints deckbuilder fans when it does not meet their expectations and puts off players already fatigued by the subgenre's abundance ([David Dunham 2026, 11:07](https://youtu.be/oipNr8RE5bA?t=667)). The conclusion is not that cards are always wrong. Avoiding them helps a game stand out, but cards are familiar, they signal a specific subgenre when that is what you want (Cultist Simulator is the example cited), and they are easy to make look good without strong art skills; the right choice depends on your goals, and Dunham was glad the question was raised because it made the game easier to market ([David Dunham 2026, 15:52](https://youtu.be/oipNr8RE5bA?t=952)).

The roguelike label itself is a signal. Zeno Rogue observes that experimental games with low production values are easier to market if they are roguelikes, which helps them find players ([Zeno Rogue 2025, 27:48](https://youtu.be/wOlSws-OI2o?t=1668)). The label can also be abused: a 2016 lightning talk complained that many iOS games call themselves roguelikes while mainly trying to take players' money and waste their time ([Tariq et al. 2016, 17:34](https://youtu.be/SDojcmObQzw?t=1054)).

### Finding an underserved niche

Two studios describe picking a niche by looking at the market first. Tabea Iseli is frank that Grimoire Groves became a non-violent, cozy roguelite for money: roguelikes tend to be dark and gritty, cozy-game players were entering dungeon crawlers through games like Hades and Don't Starve, and Steam research (estimating sales of adjacent titles over time) found nothing very close to the idea; farming sims and roguelikes already share sandbox play, resource management and simple repeating gameplay ([Tabea Iseli 2022, 2:37](https://youtu.be/ZJAgY73c8bA?t=157)). Philomena Schwab's Stray Fawn revived Dungeon Clawler after a team trip to Japan showed arcades with five floors of claw machines; with China having the most Steam users, a game built on a mechanic popular in East Asia looked promising, and two team members built it in three months ([Philomena Schwab 2024, 5:39](https://youtu.be/MTam5RT8Kn0?t=339)). In both cases the niche was a familiar thing (cozy farming, claw machines) attached to a roguelike structure, aimed at an audience the genre was not yet serving.

### How players find games: tags, data and curation

On Steam, tags are the main map. Burger notes that a game's tags (up to about 20) are ordered by user vote count, which is visible in the page source, and uses that to compute a "rogueness" score: the share of a game's tag votes on rogue-related tags. Non-traditional rogue games range from 0.1% to over 40%; traditional roguelikes cluster more narrowly and somewhat higher, with a few above 60% ([Scott Burger 2023, 17:31](https://youtu.be/IliQZm5Itng?t=1051)). Comparing whole tag-vote distributions gives a similarity score that can recommend games (Rogue's nearest match on Steam scored 79%), though Burger stresses this is a sterile mathematical metric, not a measure of quality ([Scott Burger 2023, 23:54](https://youtu.be/IliQZm5Itng?t=1434)).

From this Burger draws two proposals. Steam needs a nuanced search where players set desired tag proportions with sliders, such as some roguelike, some hacking and lots of robots, to surface games they do not already know ([Scott Burger 2023, 24:55](https://youtu.be/IliQZm5Itng?t=1495)). And because commercially successful games drown out searches, players should actively vote roguelike tags on games so the community can find them ([Scott Burger 2023, 31:49](https://youtu.be/IliQZm5Itng?t=1909)). The analysis was only possible on Steam: itch.io has about 10,000 roguelike-tagged results but no good API, and Google Play is more locked down still and does not tag games as roguelike at all ([Scott Burger 2023, 7:30](https://youtu.be/IliQZm5Itng?t=450); [Scott Burger 2023, 31:49](https://youtu.be/IliQZm5Itng?t=1909)).

Others look past tags. Santiago Zapata, who wants the word "roguelike" left loosely defined so the genre can evolve, suggests curated catalogs and communities focused on classic-style roguelikes so that people who like that kind of game can keep finding it ([Santiago Zapata 2017, 22:53](https://youtu.be/wwc7pZqs9UA?t=1373)). Lisa Brown would like games tagged by player motivation, without expecting the general audience to adopt it; meanwhile a player can ask targeted questions of a game like Hades (how long the time horizons are, how fast the failure loop, how long between decisions, how much exploration and unknown) to predict whether it will click ([Lisa Brown 2020, 27:52](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=1672)).

**In practice:** decide what your screenshots and capsule art promise and whether that matches what the game delivers. Pick a niche you can describe in Steam tags, check how crowded those tags are, and ask your players to vote the tags that fit.

## Getting found: streamers, festivals and word of mouth

The strongest convergence in the business talks is about marketing: for the roguelikes these talks describe, streamers and events sold games, and social media mostly did not.

### The streamer flywheel

Dylan Gedig and Philomena Schwab reached this conclusion independently. Gedig reports that Peglin launched with 75,000 Steam wishlists and sold twice that many copies within three weeks, far above the 10% of wishlists Gedig expected, largely because of streamers and the Steam algorithm; the community that formed came mostly from roguelike streamers' audiences, and ongoing sales still come heavily from YouTube videos that drive visits for months, with spikes from Twitch ([Dylan Gedig 2022, 3:36](https://youtu.be/ke0cLTVg2_M?t=216)). Twitter mostly reached other developers and Reddit barely moved the needle; digital events and streamers were what worked ([Dylan Gedig 2022, 9:05](https://youtu.be/ke0cLTVg2_M?t=545)). Schwab saw the same with Dungeon Clawler: with no paid campaigns, a dedicated base of roguelike YouTubers and streamers who look for new and weird roguelikes kept the game alive, while social media did little apart from one Reddit post ([Philomena Schwab 2024, 8:50](https://youtu.be/MTam5RT8Kn0?t=530)).

Gedig describes the mechanism as a flywheel. Development updates create content and moments for streams; streams bring feedback, word of mouth and sales; sales fund full-time development, which makes the game better and feeds more streaming ([Dylan Gedig 2022, 16:50](https://youtu.be/ke0cLTVg2_M?t=1010)).

> A flywheel that just builds and builds. — [Dylan Gedig 2022, 16:50](https://youtu.be/ke0cLTVg2_M?t=1010)

### Why roguelikes suit streaming

Gedig argues roguelikes fit streamers because they are endlessly replayable, update often, and are easy to hop between, so variety streamers can rotate three or four of them and layer external challenges on top: spinning a wheel to pick a game, or a "pyramid" challenge deck with constraints like winning Peglin while taking only a basic relic ([Dylan Gedig 2022, 15:11](https://youtu.be/ke0cLTVg2_M?t=911)). Peglin ships small updates every one to two weeks, first to an experimental branch, and when several roguelikes update on that cadence it gives a streamer a steady supply of video material ([Dylan Gedig 2022, 15:11](https://youtu.be/ke0cLTVg2_M?t=911)). The fit is old. At the 2016 lightning talks Casey, host of the "NetHack Nights" Twitch stream, said NetHack streams well because surprising events arise in any run, chat viewers who know the game react and advise (shouting at mistakes on a 20-second delay), and all you need is streaming software and a terminal ([Tariq et al. 2016, 6:22](https://youtu.be/SDojcmObQzw?t=382)).

### The playbook

The concrete advice from these talks is specific enough to follow:

- **Enter festivals with a demo.** Gedig tells small developers to enter every online festival they can, most of which charge no fee, and Steam Next Fest with a demo, because streamers watch festivals looking for the next roguelike; festivals also double as early playtesting, and you can only enter the Next Fest closest to release ([Dylan Gedig 2022, 20:49](https://youtu.be/ke0cLTVg2_M?t=1249)). Passing about 8,000 Steam wishlists gets a game into Steam's popular upcoming list, and Peglin won an award at the Taipei Game Show's digital event ([Dylan Gedig 2022, 9:05](https://youtu.be/ke0cLTVg2_M?t=545)).
- **Launch the demo where people are looking.** Dungeon Clawler launched its store page and demo together during Steam's Deckbuilders Fest, after 3-4 months of work, with outreach to creators who had played Stray Fawn's earlier games; wishlists tracked demo player numbers closely, though Schwab notes Steam's rules on demos and wishlists have since changed ([Philomena Schwab 2024, 7:55](https://youtu.be/MTam5RT8Kn0?t=475)). For Next Fest the studio contacted a few thousand creators, and the game became the 11th most played of that fest ([Philomena Schwab 2024, 8:50](https://youtu.be/MTam5RT8Kn0?t=530)).
- **Make the first email complete.** Put a Steam key and a GIF in your first email to a streamer and skip strict embargoes. Gedig heard back from few streamers, yet every major streamer on the list played or posted on launch day to catch the release surge; some will not stream a game until it seems ready, and all of this cost nothing ([Dylan Gedig 2022, 22:12](https://youtu.be/ke0cLTVg2_M?t=1332)).
- **Go regional where the story is.** Stray Fawn ran its PR with a Japan focus and got about ten times more coverage from Japan than from the rest of the world combined, drawn by the story of Western developers inspired by Japanese arcades; Schwab adds that this kind of game is hard to sell to press before it is already a success ([Philomena Schwab 2024, 8:29](https://youtu.be/MTam5RT8Kn0?t=509)). The studio does most PR itself but always uses external partners for China and Japan ([Philomena Schwab 2024, 14:47](https://youtu.be/MTam5RT8Kn0?t=887)).

### Other routes to an audience

An existing community can launch you. Evan Debenham posted the first release of Shattered Pixel Dungeon only to the Pixel Dungeon subreddit; the response was strong enough that the game shipped to Google Play early, and that community's attention made the game rank well there, so version 0.2.0 got over 100,000 downloads in a month ([Evan Debenham 2021, 4:21](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=261)). Debenham is careful about the cause: the community itself was the smaller early growth, and the big spike came from the store ranking its attention produced ([Evan Debenham 2021, 4:21](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=261)).

Some audiences will never download anything. Joe Sondow argues that building game-like things on social media, such as Twitter bots, reaches people who lack the patience to download an executable, trust it and run it, because things retweeted into a timeline are discovered and played in place ([Joe Sondow 2017, 9:11](https://youtu.be/4byHHDeVKoA?t=551)).

Caves of Qud made its own channel. Caelyn Sandel moved Qud's official streams to a VTuber snapjaw avatar after being mocked on face-cam as a trans woman; the weekly teaching and free-play streams are backed by the founders as a marketing expense, and the bombastic persona promotes the game while shielding Sandel from harassment ([Caelyn Sandel 2020, 18:04](https://youtu.be/NANqgqeqh2k?t=1084)). Sandel also gives keys to people who say they wish they could play Qud but are broke, targeting people likely to share the game's values, and argues that varied new materials beyond the same trailers give people who bounced off quietly a reason to look again ([Caelyn Sandel 2020, 22:50](https://youtu.be/NANqgqeqh2k?t=1370)). Ivy Melinda warns that you cannot measure what such giveaways achieve: you can count keys given and copies activated, but the connections they form are invisible in the statistics ([Ivy Melinda 2020, 27:17](https://youtu.be/db6S2lgTWmI?t=1637)).

### Streams as a design surface

If streams are where your game is seen, it is tempting to design for them directly. The two attempts in the talks show it is harder than it looks. Tyriq Plummer calls Clean Sweep's Twitch integration, which let chat control monsters, probably the game's biggest failure: drop-in viewers who don't know roguelike conventions need very readable visuals, chat needs its own view to plan surprises rather than acting in the player's sight, and chat monsters need many systems and stakes beyond chasing the player and lowering their HP, so "minimal viable fun" is not minimal ([Tyriq Plummer 2020, 28:04](https://youtu.be/neuJCYmbAG8?t=1684)). Isaac Schankler found the same lesson about complexity from the other side: the Public Modular, a synth played through Twitch chat commands, was fun but its intricate commands meant only a handful of people could take part, so Orb Pondering Simulator stripped commands down to a small set like !spawn and !kill ([Isaac Io Schankler 2024, 14:55](https://youtu.be/M6t5W5PPVW0?t=895)).

**In practice:** plan your updates, demos and festival entries around the creators who will show them. Ship small updates on a steady cadence, put a demo in every festival you can, send keys without embargoes, and spend your outreach time on streamers before social media.

## Paying for it: business models from postcardware to premium

Roguelikes have been given away, traded for postcards, sold as shareware, supported by patrons and sold at full price. The talks show what each model costs the game and how little most of them earned.

### Keep monetisation away from the challenge

Evan Debenham makes the clearest argument about what a challenging roguelike cannot sell. Ads take screen space and raise privacy concerns, and pay-for-advantage microtransactions cheapen the gameplay, which is especially damaging when the game is meant to be hard ([Evan Debenham 2021, 19:48](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=1188)). For Shattered Pixel Dungeon there was a second constraint: Pixel Dungeon had set a precedent of a fully offline game with only a tiny donate button, and because Shattered is open source, its community could take the code and compete if Debenham sold out, so any monetisation had to be non-disruptive ([Evan Debenham 2021, 19:48](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=1188)).

The solution was a ladder. In 2015 supporter purchases were added, limited to cosmetic and mild-convenience extras (custom gravestone epitaphs, renaming heroes and items, extra rankings screens, UI recolours) designed neither to cheapen the game nor to make non-buyers feel they miss out; in 2019 came a Patreon with weekly mini-blogs, content polls and an exclusive Discord, which needs constant upkeep but gives dedicated players a community ([Evan Debenham 2021, 20:56](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=1256)). Each step depended on the previous one: cosmetics earned well only while updates kept quality up, Patreon needed enough members, and selling the game outright, which looks most sustainable, became possible only once the game was worth buying ([Evan Debenham 2021, 23:08](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=1388)). Shattered launched on iOS for $5 in 2021 with seven years of content behind it, where Pixel Dungeon already cost $3 and Apple users buy up front more readily; Debenham says selling it could not have started seven years earlier ([Evan Debenham 2021, 23:08](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=1388)).

> The game has to be worth buying in the first place. I could definitely not have started selling the game seven years ago. — [Evan Debenham 2021, 23:08](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=1388)

On mobile, the developers Philomena Schwab consulted pointed the same way. When Stray Fawn planned a simultaneous mobile and PC early-access release of Dungeon Clawler, most of the roguelike developers asked, including those behind Peglin and Luck be a Landlord, recommended launching premium rather than free-to-play ([Philomena Schwab 2024, 10:58](https://youtu.be/MTam5RT8Kn0?t=658)). Schwab also found the risk on the other side: after Next Fest, three free-to-play mobile clones copied Dungeon Clawler's itemization, character designs and balancing, which hurts a premium game before it launches. The talk separates this from legitimate inspiration; another claw-machine roguelike was completely different and Schwab would happily bundle with it ([Philomena Schwab 2024, 13:14](https://youtu.be/MTam5RT8Kn0?t=794)). A simple, novel design is easy to clone, and in Schwab's case the clones were free.

### A history of modest returns

The genre's founders earned nothing from its first hit. Rogue spread because a binary reached Bell Labs, where it was renamed, and then shipped with the 4.2 Berkeley Unix distribution, so it was played across campuses without earning its authors money; Glenn Wichman's advice is that if you can get your game shipped with an operating system, take it ([Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 22:11](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=1331)).

Thomas Biskup made ADOM postcardware because there was no way to earn money from it then and Biskup enjoyed meeting people worldwide: players who liked the game paid by mailing a postcard from wherever they lived, and thousands arrived, eventually from every continent including Antarctica ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 11:59](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=719)).
