Jeff Olson, who released Alphaman as shareware about four years into development, received about 30 paid registrations and jokes the hourly wage was below Victorian child labour; Olson wishes they had asked for postcards like ADOM, since meeting people mattered more to them than the money ([Jeff Olson 2023, 18:30](https://youtu.be/Gk5uWXBANkA?t=1110)).

Selling a traditional roguelike commercially has been possible but tight. Josh Ge reports Cogmind earned about $62,000 in its first year before reaching Steam, later about $75,000, after more than three years of work: just enough for one full-time developer, or as a friend put it, going from unpaid to poorly paid ([Josh Ge 2016, 26:55](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1615)). ADOM's 2015 Steam release mattered because it generated income to pay team members working on it full-time, while Biskup personally works on it for fun ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 22:02](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=1322)).

### Edge cases

Two talks show business models bending around unusual goals. Jim Shepard's Stop the Hunger Clock drive gives donated Steam keys to players who buy hunger-relief food locally and mail in a receipt, deliberately avoiding a push-button online donation so people act in their own communities; one player who couldn't find food bags volunteered four hours at a church food drive instead ([Thomas Robertson et al. 2017, 7:06](https://youtu.be/H6fPIhLoA1Y?t=426)). Aaron Reed found that selling Subcutanean, a novel generated uniquely for each buyer, broke the distribution system: most print-on-demand services require human review of any manuscript change, which every order triggers, and Amazon requires a new ISBN whenever the text changes ([Aaron A. Reed 2020, 26:32](https://youtu.be/x0Xh4oCX9t0?t=1592)). If your product is procedural, check that the channel can carry it.

**In practice:** keep anything you sell away from the challenge, prefer premium where the genre's players expect it, and expect to earn the right to charge by building something worth buying first.

## Crowdfunding: lessons from ADOM's campaign

Almost everything the talks say about crowdfunding comes from one source: Thomas Biskup's 2017 post-mortem of ADOM's 2012 Indiegogo campaign, supported by Biskup's 2016 history of ADOM. Read it as one well-documented case with rules that transfer, not as the consensus of many developers.

The campaign had an unusual purpose. After about ten dormant years, the team used it to judge whether enough people still cared to justify restarting development. They used Indiegogo because Kickstarter was not open to Germans at the time, ran the maximum 60 days, asked for $48,000 and raised more than $90,000, which Biskup counts as a big success ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 1:52](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=112)). Work restarted in September 2012 ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 18:49](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=1129)).

### The core lessons

**Build the community first.** Biskup's main warning is that communities are not built during a campaign; without one, a campaign is likely to be nothing but a valley of desperation, and if you don't know whether you have a community, you probably shouldn't crowdfund ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 12:44](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=764)). ADOM was lucky to keep its community through ten years of hibernation, and viral million-dollar campaigns are lottery-like exceptions ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 12:44](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=764)). It is the crowdfunding form of Josh Ge's general rule that you need a community to have a successful roguelike ([Josh Ge 2016, 6:48](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=408)).

**You are your own biggest source of backers.** Analysing referral sources afterwards, Biskup found the top source of donations was the developer's own outreach, then other individuals, with Indiegogo and its front-page feature near the bottom ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 5:27](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=327)). The platform accounted for only about 1.5-2% of donations, and its front-page feature showed as a tiny one-day bump in the chart ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 25:19](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1519)).

> If you don't manage to acquire donors through your own visibility and your activities, you probably won't get them. — [Thomas Biskup 2017, 5:27](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=327)

**Set a minimal goal and add stretch goals.** The $48,000 goal tried to fund all ten planned features at once. Biskup thinks a minimum goal for one or two of the most interesting features, "barely enough to succeed", followed by interesting stretch goals would likely have funded on day five or ten instead of near the end, so that about 50 of the 60 days were not lost ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 17:02](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1022)). The evidence is what happened after funding: once backers knew the game would happen and stretch levels opened, every following day beat the valley days, and Biskup calls not anticipating this a big mistake ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 10:04](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=604)).

**Promise virtual rewards, not physical ones.** Physical rewards added in desperation, above all a pen-and-paper ADOM RPG that had to be written, checked, packaged and shipped, kept the team from programming for weeks and months; for a computer game, promise rewards inside the game ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 24:56](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1496)). In the 2016 talk Biskup adds that the RPG was delayed again and again because Biskup loves programming but hates writing, and the conclusion for any future campaign was no physical rewards at all ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 22:51](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=1371)).

### The shape of a campaign

ADOM's daily donations followed a curve Biskup describes as emotionally very hard. More than $7,000 came in the first 24 hours and 25% of the goal within three days, then donations fell to around a hundred dollars a day for weeks: the "valley of desperation" ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 6:37](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=397)). The team tried to climb out. "Power pledge drives" promised predefined extra content if a target was reached within a few days, such as +1 corruption content for every $300 donated within five days; three drives each produced a tiny, brief spike and were not worth the effort ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 7:27](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=447)). Limited, never-again-available physical rewards, first expensive boxes and then a cheaper RPG book, also gave one small spike before donations trickled back to nothing ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 8:37](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=517)).

Funding arrived only seven or eight days before the end, followed by a day almost as big as the first ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 10:04](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=604)). The last 24 hours brought in about $22,000-23,000, more than any other seven-day period, helped by a backer who pledged $5,000 if the community passed $70,000 within an hour (it took about 30 minutes) and another who matched that pledge ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 11:01](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=661)). Since the action came at the start, at funding and at the end, Biskup doubts long campaigns help: most of the time nothing happens, which is bad for morale, and shorter campaigns can work very well ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 11:43](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=703)).

The goal also drew anger. Many people thought it outrageous to ask for $48,000 ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 18:49](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=1129)), and ADOM was called greedy while cheaper campaigns promised more. Biskup believes those cheaper campaigns did not deliver, and warns against over-optimism: serious work needs money, the goal deserves long thought, and you can fail one crowdfunding campaign but not a second ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 18:12](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1092)).

### Presentation and platform

- **Video first.** The video matters more than anything else. Keep it to about 90 seconds, since nobody watches ten-minute videos, and if you cannot make an excellent one yourself, pay a videographer a thousand or two dollars or find enthusiastic community members to help ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 14:03](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=843)).
- **Visuals, even for ASCII.** After the video, backers judge by images how professional the project looks; video plus visuals is about two-thirds of a win. Biskup admits this is hard for ASCII games but cites Josh Ge's Cogmind as proof ASCII can look amazing ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 15:28](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=928)).
- **Professional text.** ADOM's community tore apart Biskup's own campaign text and rewrote it completely, which Biskup calls the best thing that could have happened; campaigns with a grammar mistake per sentence do not win people's trust with money ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 16:06](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=966)).
- **The biggest platform.** Biskup recommends Kickstarter over Indiegogo purely for visibility: if only a tiny fraction of visitors care, you want the platform with the most visitors ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 14:43](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=883)).
- **Simple pledge levels.** One exclusive $40 level that did not include the other rewards had to be explained hundreds of times, despite warnings in capital letters; make every level straightforward, with no special ideas in it ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 26:55](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1615)).

The platform's limits cost ADOM its best publicity. A joke $50,000 tier, the source code printed in leather-bound books and hand-delivered with a weekend of explanation, mocking those who had sent death threats demanding the source (a story the last section returns to), was claimed by Notch within minutes of launch ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 20:16](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=1216); [Thomas Biskup 2017, 28:14](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1694)). Indiegogo let campaigns create levels of any size, but its PayPal account could not accept more than $10,000; after days with support, Notch was asked to verify identity at a bank with a passport and declined ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 28:14](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1694)). Biskup regrets the lost publicity more than the money, judging it probably worth millions, and gives it as the reason for never using Indiegogo again ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 20:16](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=1216); [Thomas Biskup 2017, 28:14](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1694); [Thomas Biskup 2017, 14:43](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=883)).

### Running it and finishing it

The campaign took three to five hours of communication a day, across social channels, blogs, forums and mailing lists, for 60 days on top of a full-time job; Biskup prepared well and still totally underestimated it, and it became draining after the 30th or 40th day ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 21:15](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1275)). Repetition is unavoidable: Indiegogo told the team people usually need seven contacts before donating, which Biskup found about right, and even after 50 daily posts some people who checked Biskup's Facebook every day had never seen the campaign ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 22:09](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1329)). Plan every activity before launch by studying successful campaigns, because mid-campaign you will have neither the time nor the energy to invent new ones, and desperation in the valley is when things get out of hand ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 23:32](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1412)).

Expect hate for asking for money at all, and learn to ignore haters, but separate them from blunt critics. Some of ADOM's initially nasty commenters were seriously trying to improve the campaign, and engaging them produced feedback Biskup thinks the campaign might have failed without, even when it arrived as "all your texts are shit" ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 29:45](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1785)).

The money is smaller than it looks. Budget every cost in advance: a 5-10% platform share, printing, shipping and legal fees, with German lawyers typically charging about 1,800-2,400 euros a day and contracts rarely taking one day ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 19:59](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1199)). Crowdfunding income is taxed, possibly at 40-50% in some countries; ADOM's campaign ended near year-end, leaving no time to accrue costs against it, and a large tax demand arrived before any work was done, recovered only later after a tense argument ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 18:59](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1139)). Fulfilment was its own burden: in 2012 there were no automated delivery portals, so the team wrote their own, learned about UTF-8, exported addresses to label-printing programs and sometimes hand-wrote Korean addresses ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 25:42](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1542)).

One open question concerns who pays. ADOM is English-only, and almost a third of donations came from the US, with English-speaking countries first, then a strong Eastern European fanbase in Poland, Ukraine and Russia; the second-largest group was the 42 other donating countries combined. Biskup wonders whether more languages would have changed that, though the team judged translation impossible with reasonable effort ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 3:43](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=223)).

### Pre-launch checklist

Drawn from ADOM's case:

- Do you already have a community you can reach directly? If you cannot tell, don't launch yet ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 12:44](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=764)).
- Is your goal the minimum that makes the project viable, with stretch goals ready for after funding ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 17:02](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1022); [Thomas Biskup 2017, 10:04](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=604))?
- Are your rewards virtual and your pledge levels simple enough to need no explanation ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 24:56](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1496); [Thomas Biskup 2017, 26:55](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1615))?
- Do you have a 90-second video, strong visuals and professionally written text ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 14:03](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=843); [Thomas Biskup 2017, 15:28](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=928); [Thomas Biskup 2017, 16:06](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=966))?
- Have you planned every update and post for the whole campaign, and budgeted three to five hours a day to run it ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 23:32](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1412); [Thomas Biskup 2017, 21:15](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1275))?
- Have you checked that the platform can actually accept your largest pledge level ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 28:14](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1694))?
- Have you budgeted platform fees, taxes, lawyers and fulfilment, and considered when the money will land in your tax year ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 19:59](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1199); [Thomas Biskup 2017, 18:59](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1139))?

## Who owns community work: authorship, openness and culture

Much of this chapter argues that roguelikes are made collectively. That collective work sits uneasily with law, commerce and the authority of a single creator, and the talks here are less about technique than about choices a developer has to make deliberately.

### What the law sees

Kaysa Konopljak's account of DotA is the sharpest warning. In this telling, the legal system's preference for easy-to-understand singular authorship let Valve and Blizzard reframe a community mod made by many people as the work of a few hired "masterminds" ([Kaysa Konopljak 2024, 16:13](https://youtu.be/s0XCPTZDgUg?t=973)). The strategy had three prongs: declare mastermindship with an unbroken chronological line of authorship, discredit the community as unserious people with usernames, and demand that anyone else prove their claim; courts, Konopljak says, find collective works too messy to adjudicate ([Kaysa Konopljak 2024, 16:13](https://youtu.be/s0XCPTZDgUg?t=973)). The earlier contributors whose work laid the groundwork for DotA Allstars were mentioned only in passing, because they never encrypted their work or claimed it and were not in the room with the lawyers; if copyright only protects those able to enact and police ownership, they argue, the claim that it protects artists does not hold ([Kaysa Konopljak 2024, 22:38](https://youtu.be/s0XCPTZDgUg?t=1358)). The incentive this creates is corrosive: guides tell creators to keep proof-of-work timelines and hold ideas secret until they can afford lawyers, which pushes people towards anti-social, competitive behaviour and away from the collective authorship that made DotA possible ([Kaysa Konopljak 2024, 27:45](https://youtu.be/s0XCPTZDgUg?t=1665)).

Konopljak ends on roguelike developers specifically. Their transparency, open-source code, open development and habit of openly declaring inspirations are among the best defences against authorship being appropriated; Konopljak adds that ownership of player-driven emergent narratives in procedural media is weird at best ([Kaysa Konopljak 2024, 30:58](https://youtu.be/s0XCPTZDgUg?t=1858)). NetHack shows that ethos in practice. When MoMA added NetHack to its collection, the DevTeam insisted it be credited solely to "the NetHack DevTeam", not out of secrecy but because NetHack was not built by a select few ([Jesse Collet et al. 2023, 10:23](https://youtu.be/9V_CkJ66uJQ?t=623)).

### The case for keeping it closed

Thomas Biskup pulls the other way, and the reasons are worth taking seriously. Biskup originally planned to open-source ADOM at version 1.0, then declined: it is a story-driven game expressing a personal story, tens of thousands of hours had gone into it, things like Jedi knights in ADOM were unwanted, and the expectation was that variant players would bring their requests to the originator, turning joyful storytelling into a management task ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 26:46](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=1606)). The experience that shaped this was ugly. After a hint that the source might be released, some players sent persistent death threats insisting there was no right to keep it private; Biskup says the community is overwhelmingly great and such people no longer matter, but the experience changed Biskup's view on open-sourcing considerably ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 11:00](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=660)).

The two positions are not simply right and wrong. Konopljak's case is about a community's work being taken from it; Biskup's is about one author's work being demanded by a community. What you choose depends on whose work the game mostly is, and whether you want to be the steward of everything others build on it ([Kaysa Konopljak 2024, 30:58](https://youtu.be/s0XCPTZDgUg?t=1858); [Thomas Biskup 2016, 26:46](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=1606)).

### Community as culture

Some talks widen the frame from the game's community to culture itself. Tanya X. Short suggests thinking of society as a very old live-ops simulation in which you are a thread rather than a player: each person has local variables like tastes and can expose global ones others see, some bugs are hard-coded legacy, but behaviour-based bugs like racism and sexism should be fixable, even though the servers can never be taken down ([Tanya X. Short 2020, 3:12](https://youtu.be/c6FQeo5n0Bc?t=192)). Short contrasts two ways change happens. Centralised authority such as law is clear and consistent but slow, costly and inaccessible; decentralised, peer-to-peer change is faster and stronger but prone to error and sabotage, and people tend to elevate credible sources until they become a central authority again ([Tanya X. Short 2020, 6:58](https://youtu.be/c6FQeo5n0Bc?t=418)). Pixelles, the group the talk describes, uses a "ripple effect": put tools in the hands of women and other marginalised genders and let them inspire and educate their own communities through overlapping networks, something Short says Roguelike Celebration also does ([Tanya X. Short 2020, 8:32](https://youtu.be/c6FQeo5n0Bc?t=512)). The caution is about pace: culture change has enormous inertia, you influence only "one little file" such as your neighbourhood or family, and it is not a game jam but years of patient work in which minds change through real conversation ([Tanya X. Short 2020, 12:22](https://youtu.be/c6FQeo5n0Bc?t=742)).

> You can't approach it like a game jam. This is a game that takes your whole lifetime to build. — [Tanya X. Short 2020, 12:22](https://youtu.be/c6FQeo5n0Bc?t=742)

Others make the same point about the tools and forums a community runs on. JP LeBreton calls building a tool for creative work a social and political act that opens doors for new creators; LeBreton cites Playscii's use in Nauticrawl, album covers and music videos, says they would rather spend their career on tools than games, and urges others to build tools that echo their values ([JP LeBreton 2019, 21:03](https://youtu.be/MJZvWgcxV0M?t=1263)). Andrew Doull deliberately introduces Roguelike Radio guests without the credentials that might convey authority: the only qualification is having played the game and having something interesting to say, a democratising choice; the host, Alexei Pepers, added that Roguelike Celebration shares it when it looks for speakers ([Andrew Doull 2025, 5:27](https://youtu.be/NaqP13nkpfU?t=327)). For anyone starting such a channel, Doull's practical advice is to spend money on client-side recording software and a room with soft furnishings, since microphones are rarely the problem ([Andrew Doull 2025, 7:18](https://youtu.be/NaqP13nkpfU?t=438)).

Two talks look outward from the genre entirely. Michael Brough argues that treating games as a wholly new medium devalues them, because it neglects how they connect to work going back centuries, from the picaresque to Shakespeare, the same blindness behind old "are games art" debates ([Michael Brough 2025, 49:51](https://youtu.be/zDKheM-E45I?t=2991)). Max Hawkins urges roguelike developers, as experts in building realities that differ every time, to apply procedural generation to randomising real life and escaping preference loops ([Max Hawkins 2019, 12:37](https://youtu.be/anwk8b7c_s0?t=757)).

**In practice:** decide openly what you share and how you credit the people who contribute, before a dispute forces the question. Declare your inspirations, keep the record of who built what, and treat your community as a culture you help shape rather than an audience you own ([Kaysa Konopljak 2024, 27:45](https://youtu.be/s0XCPTZDgUg?t=1665); [Jesse Collet et al. 2023, 10:23](https://youtu.be/9V_CkJ66uJQ?t=623)).

## Tensions and open questions

**Niche depth or a wider audience?** The Rogue panel and David Brevik hold that a game can have inherent quality without appealing to everyone and that niches can now succeed, and Scott Burger's data shows traditional roguelikes hold their players longer ([Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 18:17](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=1097); [David Brevik 2023, 27:13](https://youtu.be/OwFrTY3IoQQ?t=1633); [Scott Burger 2023, 29:13](https://youtu.be/IliQZm5Itng?t=1753)). Thomas Biskup argues that traditional roguelikes are not mainstream successes and that reaching wider means rethinking the genre's conventions from scratch ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 2:06](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=126); [Thomas Biskup 2019, 20:44](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1244)). Josh Ge stands between them, treating polish as the bridge that carries roguelite players into traditional games ([Josh Ge 2016, 15:57](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=957); [Josh Ge 2016, 28:45](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1725)). The choice depends on whether a small, loyal audience can pay for the game, and on how much of the existing community you are prepared to unsettle.

**How close to stand to modders.** Subset Games made Into the Breach easier to mod and tries not to break mods, though it lacks time to build full tools ([Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 23:58](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=1438)); Jon Perry keeps UFO 50 mods at arm's length so they do not steer Perry's own design ([Jon Perry 2025, 31:04](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=1864)); Caves of Qud hires its modders and fan writers ([George Moromisato 2022, 22:51](https://youtu.be/mES03vaZo3U?t=1371); [Ivy Melinda 2020, 16:52](https://youtu.be/db6S2lgTWmI?t=1012)). It depends on whether you want fan work to shape the game or to run alongside it, and on how much attention you can spare.

**Open or closed authorship.** Kaysa Konopljak argues that the roguelike community's openness, open source and declared inspirations are the best defence against a collective work being appropriated ([Kaysa Konopljak 2024, 30:58](https://youtu.be/s0XCPTZDgUg?t=1858)). Biskup refused to open-source ADOM because it tells a personal story and Biskup did not want to field variant players' requests ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 26:46](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=1606)), a view hardened by death threats demanding the code ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 11:00](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=660)), and offers modding instead as a compromise ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 17:29](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=1049)). Openness also constrains business: Evan Debenham could not monetise Shattered Pixel Dungeon aggressively because its community could fork it ([Evan Debenham 2021, 19:48](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=1188)). It depends on whose work the game mostly is.

**Must scores be verified?** Drew Streib takes a hard line on restored games so that a NAO score means something, but warns that fewer people care about bragging rights than you think ([Drew Streib 2016, 6:37](https://youtu.be/J4RK-3zW8vY?t=397)). Jim Shepard would rather wipe leaderboards after a big patch and give the old champion a cosmetic hat ([Jim Shepard 2017, 29:09](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=1749)), and Alan Malloy suspects DCSS's tournament scoring rewards quantity over skill ([Alan Malloy 2017, 28:41](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=1721)). How much rigour you need depends on how large your competitive minority is.

**A unique world per player, or a common one?** Tariq and Ivy Melinda locate the value of procedural generation in the differences players compare ([Tariq et al. 2016, 2:03](https://youtu.be/SDojcmObQzw?t=123); [Ivy Melinda 2020, 7:55](https://youtu.be/db6S2lgTWmI?t=475)), while slashie set procgen aside for a non-procedural world so that discoveries could be shared ([slashie 2026, 9:12:22](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=33142)). Shared seeds are a partial middle path, which Qud's developers admit only "sort of works" ([Jason Grinblat et al. 2018, 10:15](https://youtu.be/owmGknfj6H4?t=615); [Ivy Melinda 2020, 20:07](https://youtu.be/db6S2lgTWmI?t=1207)). It depends on whether you want players to compare stories or compare findings.

**How to answer a backlash.** Subset explains its reasoning and holds to what testing supported ([Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 9:37](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=577)); Against the Storm waits two weeks before reacting ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 21:22](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=1282)); Angband's maintainers ran simulations and adjusted where the complaint held up ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 25:51](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=1551)); Blaseball openly kept a broken voting system and patched around it ([Joel Clark 2020, 32:01](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=1921)). The common ground is diagnosis before action; what follows depends on whether the evidence supports the complaint and whether the flaw is part of the game's fun.

**Streams as a design surface.** Dylan Gedig and the host of a NetHack Twitch stream agree that roguelikes stream well ([Dylan Gedig 2022, 15:11](https://youtu.be/ke0cLTVg2_M?t=911); [Tariq et al. 2016, 6:22](https://youtu.be/SDojcmObQzw?t=382)), but both attempts to let chat play directly ran into trouble, Tyriq Plummer's by its designer's own account the game's biggest failure ([Tyriq Plummer 2020, 28:04](https://youtu.be/neuJCYmbAG8?t=1684); [Isaac Io Schankler 2024, 14:55](https://youtu.be/M6t5W5PPVW0?t=895)). How to design for a stream audience, rather than simply be streamable, is unsolved.

**Problems nobody has solved.** How to find an audience for a game that fits no existing one ([Various 2018, 41:15](https://youtu.be/60MTG-__dt4?t=2475)); how to measure what a key giveaway achieves ([Ivy Melinda 2020, 27:17](https://youtu.be/db6S2lgTWmI?t=1637)); whether translation would have widened ADOM's backers ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 3:43](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=223)); how players can show off unique procedural creations inside the game ([Gabriel Koenig 2020, 20:55](https://youtu.be/xju91VGh2Ps?t=1255)); and who owns player-driven emergent narratives at all ([Kaysa Konopljak 2024, 30:58](https://youtu.be/s0XCPTZDgUg?t=1858)).

## Checklist

1. Can a player share a run, a death or a single generated thing in one action, and have you looked at your output at that cropped scale?
2. Does the game write a log, morgue or scrollback that someone else can read as a story, and can players enter a seed?
3. What game data could you expose publicly without touching personal or login information?
4. If the game went online, what would spectating, shared bones or scoreboards add, and what must a score prove?
5. What does a balance patch do to existing records?
6. Is your content in data files that a modder can change in a few lines, and will those mods survive your updates?
7. Have you left deliberate gaps for modders, and decided how closely you will look at what they make?
8. How often do you release, and how many clicks does it take a player to send you feedback?
9. When you act on feedback, does the player who gave it find out?
10. For each complaint, do you know the desire behind it, and whether it is a design problem, a presentation problem or a request for a different game?
11. Who is not talking, and how will you weigh them before reversing a change?
12. How many hours a week does community work take, who sets the tone, and what can volunteers do?
13. Who is your main audience, and do your art, screenshots and tags promise what the game delivers?
14. Which streamers and festivals will see your next update or demo?
15. Does anything you sell touch the challenge, and if you crowdfund, do you already have a community you can reach directly?
